sections.text: ## The Big Picture

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text: A reef is a carbonate structure built by organisms faster than it is destroyed by physical and biological erosion. The key insight: reefs are not passive rock — they are dynamic accretion systems in near-equilibrium. Remove the animals and the reef erodes away within decades.

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
```
REEF BUDGET: ACCRETION vs. EROSION
====================================

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
ACCRETION SIDE                     EROSION SIDE
--------------                     ------------
Coral calcification (primary)       Bioerosion (sponges bore into skeleton)
Coralline algae (encrusting)        Parrotfish (scrape coral surface)
Mollusks, serpulid worms            Sea urchins (rasp substrate)
Foraminifera (sand-forming)         Chemical dissolution (low Ωarag)
                                    Storm breakage and abrasion

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text: NET REEF GROWTH WHEN:  Accretion rate > Erosion rate

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
Healthy reef:      1–10 mm/yr net vertical accretion
Degraded reef:     Net erosion — reef loses structural height
After bleaching:   Often net erosion for 5–10 years during recovery

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
Production:  2–4 kg CaCO3 m⁻² yr⁻¹ on healthy reef
Erosion:     1–2 kg CaCO3 m⁻² yr⁻¹ typical
```

sections.text: ## Carbonate Accretion Chemistry

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text: The fundamental reaction coral polyps drive to build their aragonite skeleton:

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
```
CALCIFICATION REACTION
======================

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
Ca²⁺ (seawater) + 2HCO₃⁻ (seawater) → CaCO₃ (aragonite) + H₂O + CO₂
                                              ↑
                                    secreted by polyp into
                                    extracellular calcifying fluid

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
Aragonite vs. Calcite:
- Both are CaCO₃ polymorphs
- Aragonite: orthorhombic crystal structure, denser, more soluble
- Corals exclusively use aragonite
- Coralline algae use high-Mg calcite (slightly different properties)
- Aragonite more vulnerable to dissolution as pH drops (ocean acidification)

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
The polyp drives calcification by:
1. Pumping Ca²⁺ into calcifying fluid (active transport)
2. Pumping H⁺ OUT (raising pH at deposition site)
3. Concentrating CO₃²⁻ to exceed saturation threshold
4. Organic matrix proteins template crystal growth
```

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text: **Role of zooxanthellae in calcification**: Symbiotic algae accelerate calcification 2–3× by consuming CO₂ (photosynthesis shifts equilibrium toward carbonate), providing ATP, and removing phosphate that would otherwise inhibit calcification. In darkness, corals still calcify but at 20–30% of light-enhanced rate.

sections.text: ## Builders of the Reef

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
```
REEF BUILDERS BY CONTRIBUTION
==============================

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text: PRIMARY FRAMEWORK BUILDERS:

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
Scleractinian corals (bulk of reef architecture):
  +---------------------------+
  | - Massive (brain, star)   |
  | - Branching (Acropora)    |
  | - Plating/foliose         |
  +---------------------------+
    Massive: centuries-old heads, bulk CaCO₃.
    Branching: fastest linear growth, complex structure.
    Plating/foliose: low-light adapted, slope/wall zones.

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
Crustose coralline algae (CCA):
  +---------------------------+
  | Lithothamnion             |
  | Porolithon                |
  | Hydrolithon               |
  +---------------------------+
    Bind the framework; cement loose rubble.
    Critical on reef crest (survives surge).
    Encrust dead coral, create hard substrate.

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text: SECONDARY CONTRIBUTORS:

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
+---------------------------+
  | Mollusks (giant clams,    |
  |  serpulid tube worms)     |
  | Foraminifera              |
  | Halimeda green algae      |
  | Sponges                   |
  +---------------------------+
    Mollusks: local aragonite additions.
    Foraminifera: major sand production (pink/white sand).
    Halimeda: major sediment; segments calcified.
    Sponges: bioerode AND sometimes bind rubble.
```

sections.text: **Hermatypic vs. ahermatypic corals**:

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
| Feature | Hermatypic | Ahermatypic |
|---------|-----------|-------------|
| Zooxanthellae | Present | Absent |
| Primary energy | Photosynthesis (via symbiont) | Heterotrophy only |
| Depth range | Photic zone (0–50 m) | Deep/cold; any depth |
| Reef building | Primary builders | Mound-builders only |
| Geographic range | Tropical/subtropical | Global (Norway to poles) |
| Example | Acropora, Porites, Montastraea | Lophelia pertusa, Caryophyllia |
| Temperature sensitivity | High | Low |

sections.text: ## Darwin's Subsidence Theory — The Three Stages

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text: Darwin aboard HMS Beagle (1835–1836) proposed the fringing → barrier → atoll progression based on volcanic island subsidence. Confirmed 100 years later by deep drilling on Bikini Atoll (1952) and Enewetak (1952), finding coral limestone thousands of meters thick over basalt.

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
```
DARWIN'S ATOLL FORMATION SEQUENCE
===================================

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
STAGE 1: FRINGING REEF
  Active volcano
      ___
     /   \
    | VOL |
    |CANO |____sea level
     \___/
  coral fringe
  adjacent to shore
  No lagoon (or very narrow)
  Examples: Hawaii, young Caribbean islands

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
STAGE 2: BARRIER REEF
  Island subsiding + reef tracks sea level
      ___
     /   \
    |     |__________sea level
     \___/ ~ lagoon ~
           |REEF|
  Lagoon forms between island and crest
  Reef keeps pace with subsidence by upward growth
  Examples: Great Barrier Reef (continental scale),
            Bora Bora (classic volcanic barrier)

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
STAGE 3: ATOLL
  Island fully submerged; reef ring remains
  ~~~~~~~~~~~sea level~~~~~~~~~~~
  ~ ~ ~  lagoon  ~ ~ ~
 |REEF|            |REEF|
  Ring of reef over submerged seamount
  May have sand cay (island) on windward side
  Examples: Bikini, Enewetak, Maldives, Tuamotu

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
TIMESCALE: thousands to millions of years
DRILLING:  Enewetak — 1,405 m of coral limestone over basalt
           Bikini    — ~800 m coral limestone
```

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text: **Why reefs track sea level**: Zooxanthellae require light. As the island subsides or sea level rises, the reef grows upward to maintain position in the photic zone. This "keep-up" growth is the mechanism that traces Darwin's entire sequence.

sections.text:

```
REEF RESPONSE TO SEA LEVEL CHANGE
===================================

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
SEA LEVEL RISE RATE
                   Slow (<2 mm/yr)    Fast (>10 mm/yr)

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
REEF GROWTH     +-------------+      +-------------+
RATE            |             |      |             |
High            |  KEEP UP    |      | KEEP UP or  |
(>10 mm/yr)     | reef at     |      | GIVE UP if  |
                | sea surface |      | extremely   |
                |             |      | fast        |
                +-------------+      +-------------+
Low             |             |      |             |
(<2 mm/yr)      | CATCH UP    |      | GIVE UP     |
                | drowned flat|      | submerged   |
                | reef visible|      | reef = guyot|
                +-------------+      +-------------+

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
"Drowned reefs":  Submerged structures attesting to past rapid sea level rise
                  Found at 20–40m depth on GBR; Florida shelf edge reefs
                  Date to Holocene rapid rise events (Meltwater Pulse 1A)

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
CURRENT concern:  Sea level rise ~3.6 mm/yr (accelerating post-2000)
                  Degraded reefs (low accretion) vulnerable to drowning
```

```
sections.text:
MORPHOLOGY        SPECIES EXAMPLES          LINEAR GROWTH   NOTES
--------------    ----------------------    -------------   -----
Massive / brain   Porites lobata            5–25 mm/yr      Centuries old
                  Diploria labyrinthica                     possible; annual
                  Orbicella annularis                       bands in X-ray
                                                            (paleoclimate proxy)
Columnar          Porites compressa         10–30 mm/yr     Dense; high

                                                            disturbance regimes

                                                            deep slope zones
Branching         Acropora muricata         100–200 mm/yr   Fragile; fast
                  Acropora hyacinthus                       structural recovery
                  Pocillopora damicornis    50–100 mm/yr    Less extreme
Staghorn          Acropora cervicornis      100–200 mm/yr   Caribbean dominant;
(Caribbean)                                                 reduced >95% since
                                                            1970s; now listed
```

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text: Note: "growth rate" is tip extension for branching; bulk CaCO₃ output matters more for reef accretion. A massive *Porites* head contributes more limestone per year than a fast-growing branching coral despite slower linear extension.

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text: **Age and size**: Massive *Porites* heads can be 5–10 m diameter, 500–700 years old. Annual growth bands visible in X-radiograph of core slabs — analogous to tree rings. GBR *Porites* cores provide continuous paleoclimate records extending to the 1600s (SST, rainfall proxies).

sections.text: ## Decision Cheat Sheet

metadata.title: Reef Formation: Carbonate Accretion, Atoll Development, Sea Level

sections.text:
| If you need to diagnose... | Start With | Key Caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Coral skeleton mineral | Aragonite CaCO3 polymorph | Aragonite saturation state, not pH alone, controls precipitation tendency. |
| Atoll origin | Darwin's fringing-to-barrier-to-atoll subsidence sequence | Requires reef growth to keep pace with subsidence. |
| Framework cement | Crustose coralline algae on wave-beaten crests | CCA is structural, not decorative. |
| Branching coral recovery | 100-200 mm/yr tip extension | Fast growth is fragile and storm-sensitive. |
| Massive coral growth | 5-25 mm/yr extension with large bulk carbonate output | Slow extension can still build substantial CaCO3. |
| Net reef accretion | Healthy 1-10 mm/yr versus net erosion on degraded reefs | Accretion is growth plus cement minus bioerosion and storms. |
| Sea-level tracking | Zooxanthellae light demand and upward photic-zone growth | Turbidity, temperature, and chemistry can prevent tracking. |
| Drowned reef interpretation | Reef unable to keep pace with sea-level rise | Drowned reefs are submerged relics, not active catch-up systems. |
| Ahermatypic growth | Heterotrophy without zooxanthellae in deep/cold water | These corals do not build tropical photic reefs the same way. |
| Porites paleoclimate archive | 500-700 year heads with annual bands | Bands are proxies and require careful calibration. |
